newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Eurostocks rebound after Tokyo reassurance.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Eurostocks rebound after Tokyo reassurance.

text.p: European bourses, their confidence stiffened by Japanese government reassurances, bounced back on Tuesday from sharp early losses sparked by Wall Street's second largest points plunge ever.

Stocks in London, Frankfurt and Paris were marked down heavily after the Dow Jones industrials tumbled 192 points, or 2.5 percent, overnight. The sell-off was caused by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's remarks about potential Japanese sales of U.S. government bonds.

The dollar also fell more than one yen when Hashimoto, responding to a question after a speech in New York, said Japan had in the past been tempted to sell its holdings of U.S. government bonds and boost its gold reserves, but had not done so.

But the European markets steadied after Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Tuesday that Hashimoto had been incorrectly reported. "The prime minister's real intention was not reported correctly," he said.

A senior finance ministry said American government bonds were an essential investment tool in Japan's foreign reserves. Japanese purchases of U.S. bonds on a large scale has helped support Wall Street's record-breaking bull run, hence the markets dismay at talk of sales by Tokyo.

The soothing words seemed to calm volatile markets. The London stock market clawed back opening losses of 0.8 percent and Paris climbed nearly one percent after starting down 0.5 percent. The dollar recovered almost to Monday's levels after falling overnight to 114.10 yen.

London's blue-chip FTSE index's recent weak performance, which has seen it retreat 4.5 percent from its June 13 closing high, limited the severity of Tuesday's early markdown. But the recovery came in thin trade.
"People felt the early fall was an over-reaction and the Japanese are backtracking on what prime minister said so we were never going to stay down," one dealer said. "But the volume is not there."
"London's been pulling back six days on the trot," one said. "It's more important to look at the Wall Street fall in percentage terms, which is not so dramatic."
Dealers said the market would remain edgy ahead of the Wall Street opening, in case the Dow's slide proved to be more than just a one-day setback.
"More important than the early mark-down is how people react towards the open on Wall Street this afternoon," one said.

"It remains to be seen how much pain or fear the (U.S.) mutual fund holders will take before they suddenly think it's time to get out," he said. "Hitherto every fallback on Wall Street has been regarded as a buying opportunity. But one or two people are getting slightly sceptical."

The FTSE's six-day losing streak was provoked by concern about higher interest rates and the new Labour government's July 2 budget, which may abolish tax breaks on dividend payments for big institutional investors like pension funds.
French stocks made the best recovery, climbing 0.9 percent by lunch-time after the Japanese finance ministry's remarks, which helped wipe out opening index losses.

State-controlled French bank Credit Lyonnais was among the biggest early gainers with a 4.50 percent jump after a newspaper report that it expected a two billion franc ($343.7 million) profit for 1997 after a cost-cutting programme.
Frankfurt recovered from a weak opening after Wall Street to show modest gains by lunch-time. The dollar's recovery helped but volumes remained thin with little corporate news to give direction.
In currency markets, the dollar rebounded to 114.70 yen by midday from overnight lows of 114.10 when Hashimoto's remarks sent markets reeling. It was at 115.31 yen in late Europe trade on Monday.

"Markets were hit quite badly. We will now see a period characterised by denial and rebuttal from Japan. And by the time the U.S. opens this afternoon there should be a renewed calm and stability," said Julian Fisher, economist at Daiwa Europe. "I wouldn't be surprised if we saw some bounce-back both in the dollar and in the treasury markets."

Analysts said Hashimoto's comments reflected Japan's frustration at American warnings that Japan should not let its trade surplus balloon again. U.S. President Bill Clinton warned Japan on Sunday that it risks an economic war with the U.S. if the surplus explodes again.
CURRENCIES AT 1100 GMT
The dollar was at 1.7237 marks and 114.70 yen, compared with 1.7210 and 115.31 in late European trade on Monday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1100 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 11.5 points at 4,587.3.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was up 26.16 points at 2,788.36.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was up 2.82 at 3757.54.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $338.65 against $338.90 at the close on Monday. Silver was at $4.81, up two cents.
($ = 5.818 French Francs)
